back.body: INJURY IS ENERGY TRANSFERRED INTO TISSUE · SPEED MATTERS FAR MORE THAN WEIGHT — double the speed, roughly four times the energy · BLUNT: energy spread wide → serious INTERNAL injury with LITTLE TO SEE · PENETRATING: energy along a PATH → ask what is on the line between entry and where it stopped · THE SIZE OF THE HOLE TELLS YOU NOTHING · THREE COLLISIONS: vehicle into object → occupant into vehicle → ORGANS INTO THE INSIDE OF THE BODY · LOOK AT THE VEHICLE BEFORE IT IS TOWED: starred windscreen, bent wheel, intruded door · Mechanism raises suspicion — it NEVER replaces assessment
back.why_it_matters: Something bent that steering wheel and starred that windscreen, and that something was him.

front.title: Index of suspicion
front.summary: What you expect before you find anything

back.body: RAISED BY: ejection · DEATH OF ANOTHER OCCUPANT · falls · rollover · compartment intrusion · pedestrian or motorcyclist struck · NUMERIC THRESHOLDS COME FROM YOUR LOCAL TRAUMA TRIAGE CRITERIA — they vary and get revised, so use yours · OLDER PATIENTS ARE INJURED BY FAR LESS ENERGY — A FALL FROM STANDING IS A REAL MECHANISM AT 82 · CHILDREN compensate beautifully and then crash · ANTICOAGULANTS: same mechanism, much more bleeding · IT CHANGES: how hard you assess · how early you decide to go · what you say at handover · 'I FEEL FINE' DOES NOT LOWER IT
back.why_it_matters: A metre off the bottom step does not sound like a mechanism. At 82, on a blood thinner, it is one.

back.body: FOUR TIERS, IN ORDER · 1 PHYSIOLOGICAL: abnormal vitals or reduced consciousness NOW — outranks every theory · 2 ANATOMICAL: penetrating head/neck/torso, 2+ long bones, flail chest, pelvic fracture, amputation, paralysis · 3 MECHANISM: well-looking patient, enormous energy · 4 SPECIAL: age either end, ANTICOAGULATED, pregnant, burns — THE TIER MOST OFTEN SKIPPED · UNDER-TRIAGE IS FAR WORSE THAN OVER-TRIAGE, so the criteria are deliberately cautious — hesitating? Go to the trauma centre · TIME TO DEFINITIVE CARE beats geographical nearest · THE NUMBERS ARE YOUR LOCAL PROTOCOL'S, NOT A REMEMBERED ONE
back.why_it_matters: Under-triage costs an hour of transfer. Over-triage cost them fourteen minutes of driving.

back.body: See the algorithm card. Physiological → anatomical → mechanism → special considerations. A yes at any tier means trauma centre per local criteria, with a pre-alert. Only a no at all four goes to the closest appropriate facility.
back.why_it_matters: The fourth box is the one people never reach, because they stop looking after the third.

front.title: Golden period, platinum ten
front.summary: Do only what cannot be done moving

back.body: DEFINITIVE CARE = A SURGEON AND BLOOD — neither is on your ambulance · Every scene minute is a minute the treatment is not happening · The 'golden HOUR' is a TEACHING IDEA, not a biological deadline — time matters continuously, no cliff edge · PLATINUM TEN MINUTES = target scene time in major trauma · ON SCENE ONLY: failing AIRWAY · CATASTROPHIC BLEEDING · EXTRICATION · EN ROUTE: vitals, splinting, bandaging, secondary survey, history · LOAD AND GO IS GOOD CARE when the problem is inside the abdomen · Long scene times = SEQUENTIAL work, not slow movement — work in PARALLEL, do not rush
back.why_it_matters: Nobody rushed and nobody made a mistake. The eleven minutes were the mistake.

front.title: External bleeding control
front.summary: Press hard, one spot, and do not look

back.body: ARTERIAL = bright red, SPURTS with the pulse · VENOUS = darker, steady flow · CAPILLARY = oozes · CATASTROPHIC BLEEDING COMES BEFORE THE AIRWAY — it kills faster · DIRECT PRESSURE works when it is FIRM · FOCUSED ON ONE POINT · and HELD · Two fingertips on the bleeding point beat a palm on a wad of gauze · DO NOT LIFT THE DRESSING TO LOOK — every look tears apart what was forming · SOAKED THROUGH? ADD ON TOP and press harder — never remove · LIMB, pressure failing → TOURNIQUET, no hesitation · JUNCTIONAL (groin, armpit, neck) → PACK IT · ELEVATION AND PRESSURE POINTS ARE NO LONGER PRIMARY MEASURES
back.why_it_matters: It had not stopped. It had been starting to stop, twelve separate times.

front.title: Tourniquets
front.summary: Too loose is worse than none

back.body: FOR: life-threatening LIMB bleeding pressure has not controlled · pressure impractical · AMPUTATION · PROPERLY APPLIED TOURNIQUETS ARE SAFE — patients die from LATE ones, they rarely lose limbs to prompt ones · HIGH AND TIGHT above the wound · over a SINGLE BONE · NEVER OVER A JOINT · TIGHTEN UNTIL BLEEDING STOPS *AND* THE DISTAL PULSE IS GONE — both · TOO LOOSE BLOCKS VEINS BUT NOT ARTERIES AND MAKES BLEEDING WORSE — bleeding increased? TIGHTEN, do not remove · One not enough? SECOND ABOVE THE FIRST · IT WILL HURT — that is not a reason to loosen · NEVER COVER IT · WRITE THE TIME · NO FIELD RELEASE
back.why_it_matters: Everything about that tourniquet was right except that nobody could see it.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: recognise the indication, HIGH AND TIGHT over a single bone, NEVER over a joint, tighten until BLEEDING STOPS AND DISTAL PULSE GONE, tighten further if bleeding increases, second tourniquet above the first if needed, WRITE THE TIME, NEVER COVER IT, do not loosen for pain, NO FIELD RELEASE, say 'tourniquet applied at [time]' out loud at handover.
back.why_it_matters: The two failures are applying it too loosely, and hiding it under a blanket.

front.title: Wound packing
front.summary: Tight, onto the source, and commit

back.body: FOR JUNCTIONAL WOUNDS a tourniquet cannot reach: GROIN · ARMPIT · NECK · deep torso-boundary wounds · NOT THE CHEST, NOT THE ABDOMEN — a cavity has no floor to pack against · FINGER IN, FIND THE BLEEDING POINT, PACK DIRECTLY ONTO IT · KEEP FEEDING GAUZE IN — far more than you expect · FILL THE WHOLE CAVITY TIGHTLY — loose packing is FAILED packing, just wet gauze · HEMOSTATIC GAUZE PACKS THE SAME WAY — the agent shortens the time, it does not pack itself · HOLD for the specified time WITHOUT LETTING GO · Secure with a pressure dressing · DO NOT REMOVE TO LOOK · GET HANDS TO HOLD THEM FIRST — this hurts more than almost anything
back.why_it_matters: It hurt twice, because the first time was gentle.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-06-02-03. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: confirm the site (junctional, NOT chest or abdomen), get help to hold them BEFORE starting, finger in to find the source, pack DIRECTLY ONTO the bleeding point, keep feeding gauze, fill the cavity TIGHTLY, fist and body weight pressure, HOLD the full time without looking, secure with a pressure dressing, do NOT remove to inspect.
back.why_it_matters: Half-packing a wound means doing it twice, and twice hurts more than committing once.

back.body: CANNOT BE SEEN · CANNOT BE MEASURED · CANNOT BE FIXED BY YOU · WHERE IT HIDES: the floor, the CHEST, the ABDOMEN, the PELVIS, the THIGHS — litres, with nothing visible · RECOGNISE FROM MECHANISM: blunt abdominal, fall from height, crash with intrusion, penetrating torso, rib or pelvic fractures · AND FROM SHOCK, IN ORDER: RISING PULSE first → pale cool clammy → anxious → confused → quiet → THIRST → PRESSURE FALLS LAST · A NORMAL PRESSURE MEANS COMPENSATION, NOT SAFETY · BRUISING TAKES HOURS — its absence means nothing now · CARE: oxygen · KEEP WARM · position · nothing by mouth · GO TO A SURGEON
back.why_it_matters: The pulse and the hands were the only honest findings in the room.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-06-02-04. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: SHOCK = INADEQUATE PERFUSION — low pressure is ONE LATE SIGN, not the definition · COMPENSATED: fast pulse · pale cool clammy · anxious · PRESSURE STILL NORMAL because the body is working flat out — THIS IS THE TRAP AND THE MOMENT TO ACT · DECOMPENSATED: pressure falls, mental status drops — LATE AND OMINOUS · CHILDREN HOLD THEIR PRESSURE AND THEN CRASH — a normal BP in an injured child is not reassurance · THE THREE THINGS YOU CAN DO: STOP EXTERNAL BLEEDING · KEEP THEM WARM · GET THEM TO A SURGEON · COLD BLOOD DOES NOT CLOT — blankets are a clotting intervention · SUPINE unless breathing prevents it; head-down is NOT routine · Nothing by mouth however thirsty
back.why_it_matters: Children hold their pressure until they cannot. The number tells you last.

front.title: Compensated vs decompensated
front.summary: The pressure is the last thing to change

back.body: See the comparison rows. Everything except the blood pressure has already changed by the time compensated shock is established — pulse, skin, capillary refill, mental status. Act in the left column.
back.why_it_matters: Compensated shock is a patient sprinting to stand still, and they cannot keep it up.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-06-02-05. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Most bleeds come from the FRONT of the septum and are fixable on a sofa · SIT UP AND LEAN FORWARD — NEVER TILT BACK, which sends blood into the stomach and brings it back as vomit · PINCH THE SOFT PART, NOT THE BONY BRIDGE · HOLD TEN MINUTES WITHOUT CHECKING · DO NOT PACK · ASK ABOUT ANTICOAGULANTS — heavier, longer, more often needs hospital · POSTERIOR BLEED: correct technique, little from the front, but they keep SWALLOWING → hospital · AFTER HEAD TRAUMA WITH CLEAR FLUID: DO NOT PACK, DO NOT PINCH — possible skull base fracture; let it drain · A nosebleed CAN cause shock in an older anticoagulated patient
back.why_it_matters: It had been going into her stomach for half an hour, and her stomach finally had enough of it.

back.body: CLOSED = damage under INTACT SKIN, so severity is easy to miss · CONTUSION = bruise · HEMATOMA = a collection, and a big one holds real volume · BRUISING TAKES HOURS — smooth skin an hour after an impact tells you NOTHING · CRUSH: the limb is a sealed container while the weight is on — patient often stable and talking · THE DANGER IS AT RELEASE: potassium · acid · muscle breakdown all wash in at once → FATAL RHYTHMS and KIDNEY FAILURE · TELL THE RESCUE TEAM RELEASE IS A CLINICAL EVENT · COMPARTMENT SYNDROME: PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION is the earliest sign · pain on passive stretch · tight woody feel · A PRESENT PULSE EXCLUDES NOTHING
back.why_it_matters: The hour under the weight was survivable. The moment it came off needed everybody watching.

back.body: ABRASION = surface scraped, painful and dirty · LACERATION = a cut; DEPTH matters more than length · AVULSION = flap still attached → REPLACE IT IN POSITION and dress it there, it may survive · AMPUTATION = pressure, then tourniquet · PUNCTURE = tiny mark, deep track — THE HOLE SIZE MEANS NOTHING · IMPALED OBJECT STAYS IN — it may be the only thing holding the vessel closed · STABILISE with bulky dressings built around it · pressure BESIDE it, never on it · TWO EXCEPTIONS ONLY: blocks the AIRWAY, or prevents CHEST COMPRESSIONS · CSM distal, BEFORE and AFTER dressing
back.why_it_matters: Awkward is not one of the exceptions. There are only two.

front.title: Dressing and bandaging
front.summary: The limb keeps swelling; the bandage does not

back.body: DRESSING covers the wound · BANDAGE holds the dressing on and can apply pressure — two jobs · Dressings STERILE where possible and BIGGER than the wound · Bandage FIRM but never circulation-compromising · CHECK CSM AFTER APPLYING AND AGAIN IN TRANSPORT — SWELLING CONTINUES, so a correct bandage can become a tourniquet · BANDAGE DISTAL → PROXIMAL on a limb · LEAVE FINGERS AND TOES EXPOSED so checking costs nothing · NEVER CIRCUMFERENTIALLY AROUND A NECK · OCCLUSIVE DRESSINGS where air must be kept out: OPEN CHEST WOUNDS · large neck wounds · EVISCERATION
back.why_it_matters: Nothing was done wrong on scene. The swelling simply carried on happening.

front.title: Amputated part care
front.summary: Cool, never frozen; never complete a partial

back.body: PATIENT BEFORE PART — control the STUMP first: pressure, then TOURNIQUET · Handle gently — DO NOT clean, scrub or pick at it · WRAP DRY AND STERILE → SEAL IN A PLASTIC BAG → BAG ON ICE or in iced water · THE PART MUST NEVER TOUCH ICE AND MUST NEVER FREEZE — freezing destroys it · NO DRY ICE · DO NOT SOAK IT · LABEL with name and TIME OF AMPUTATION · Part not found? TRANSPORT THE PATIENT, let it follow · PARTIAL AMPUTATION: NEVER COMPLETE IT — that strand may be carrying the blood supply · support, dress, splint
back.why_it_matters: It sat in direct contact with ice for thirty-five minutes. The bag was the only thing that would have saved it.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-06-03-04. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: STUMP FIRST, wrap the part DRY and sterile, SEAL IN A BAG, bag on ice, NEVER let it touch ice or freeze, no soaking, LABEL with name and time of amputation, transport the patient even if the part is missing, and NEVER complete a partial amputation — support, dress and splint it instead.
back.why_it_matters: Two absolutes, both broken with good intentions: freezing the part, and tidying up something barely attached.

back.body: SUPERFICIAL: outer layer only · RED · DRY · painful · NO BLISTERS (sunburn) · PARTIAL THICKNESS: into the dermis · BLISTERS · moist · mottled pink/red · INTENSELY PAINFUL · FULL THICKNESS: all layers · WHITE, waxy, leathery or CHARRED · DRY · PAINLESS — the nerve endings are gone · NEVER GRADE A BURN BY HOW MUCH IT HURTS — it is backwards · Full thickness is usually RINGED by partial thickness, which is where their pain comes from · Burns are MIXED and depth DECLARES ITSELF OVER DAYS — describe, do not commit · EXTENT COUNTS PARTIAL + FULL ONLY · CIRCUMFERENTIAL FULL THICKNESS CONSTRICTS — limb circulation, chest breathing
back.why_it_matters: The part that did not hurt was the part that needed a surgeon.

front.title: Burn depth at a glance
front.summary: What to look for and what to count

back.body: SUPERFICIAL = outer layer — red, dry, NO blisters — NOT COUNTED in extent · PARTIAL THICKNESS = into the dermis — BLISTERS, moist, very painful — COUNTED · FULL THICKNESS = all layers — white/leathery/charred, DRY, PAINLESS — COUNTED · PAIN AS A SEVERITY GUIDE: INVERTED, the worst hurt least · CIRCUMFERENTIAL FULL THICKNESS: CONSTRICTS as the tissue beneath swells — check distal circulation, watch breathing on a chest
back.why_it_matters: Counting the sunburn on their shoulders inflates the number and can get them over-treated.

front.title: Rule of nines
front.summary: Adults and infants differ at the head

back.body: ADULT: head+neck 9 · EACH ARM 9 · EACH LEG 18 · front trunk 18 · back trunk 18 · genitalia 1 = 100 · A LEG IS A FIFTH OF THE BODY — people underestimate legs · INFANT: HEAD 18 (double) · each arm 9 · EACH LEG 14 · front trunk 18 · back trunk 18 · A child's head is a far bigger share and the legs a smaller one · IN BETWEEN? NO CLEAN RULE — count palms, describe exactly what is burned, let hospital use a Lund-Browder chart · PALM METHOD: THE PATIENT'S palm ≈ 1% — for scattered burns · USE THEIRS, NOT YOURS · SUPERFICIAL BURNS DO NOT COUNT · It is an ESTIMATE
back.why_it_matters: An honest description beat a confident wrong number.

front.title: Rule of nines: the figures
front.summary: Adult and infant, side by side

back.body: ADULT — head+neck 9% · each arm 9% · EACH LEG 18% · front trunk 18% · back trunk 18% · genitalia 1% · INFANT — HEAD 18% · each arm 9% · EACH LEG 14% · front trunk 18% · back trunk 18% · AGES IN BETWEEN: deliberately not printed — no clean rule exists and sources differ; use palms and a description · PALM METHOD: the PATIENT'S palm ≈ 1% (sources differ on whether fingers are included) · COUNT PARTIAL + FULL THICKNESS ONLY
back.why_it_matters: The head is where adult and infant figures part company, and it parts by double.

front.title: Burn types
front.summary: Stop the burning, then be careful how

back.body: ALL TYPES: STOP THE BURNING PROCESS FIRST · THERMAL: away from source, remove hot/smouldering clothing (leave what is stuck), COOL BRIEFLY with room-temperature water — then DRY, COVER AND KEEP WARM · TOO LONG = HYPOTHERMIA, especially children and big burns · CHEMICAL: BRUSH DRY POWDER OFF FIRST, then IRRIGATE copiously and at length · remove contaminated clothing · NEVER NEUTRALISE — the reaction makes HEAT · ELECTRICAL: the two visible wounds are ENTRY AND EXIT — all the damage is BETWEEN them · expect CARDIAC ARREST and RHYTHMS · FRACTURES from muscle contraction · NEVER TOUCH UNTIL ISOLATION IS CONFIRMED BY SOMEONE QUALIFIED · RADIATION: TIME, DISTANCE, SHIELDING — do not enter
back.why_it_matters: Two coin-sized marks, and everything on the line between them had been in the path.

back.body: See the comparison rows. Chemical: brush dry first, irrigate at length, NEVER neutralise. Electrical: never approach until isolation is CONFIRMED, and treat it as a crush injury plus a cardiac event with two small doors on it.
back.why_it_matters: One rule stops you making the burn worse. The other stops you becoming the second patient.

front.title: Inhalation injury
front.summary: The patient in front of you is not the one who will arrive

back.body: IT KILLS MORE BURN PATIENTS THAN THE SKIN BURNS DO, often with barely any external burn · THE STORY: ENCLOSED-SPACE fire · trapped · unconscious · found inside · THE FACE: SOOT round mouth and nose · SINGED facial or nasal hair · face or neck burns · THE VOICE: HOARSENESS · stridor · brassy cough · carbon in sputum · trouble swallowing · drooling — these mean it is ALREADY SWELLING · SWELLING DEVELOPS OVER MINUTES TO HOURS — patent now predicts nothing · TREATMENT IS TIME: GO EARLY, PRE-ALERT EARLY · HIGH-FLOW O2 · THE OXIMETER LIES AFTER A FIRE · Assume CO, consider cyanide · Sit up, keep calm, MINIMISE INSTRUMENTATION
back.why_it_matters: He was entirely comfortable, and that told nobody anything about the next forty minutes.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-06-04-04. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: establish the story, look at the face for soot and singeing, LISTEN to the voice, high-flow oxygen, do NOT trust the oximeter, assume carbon monoxide, sit them up, MINIMISE AIRWAY INSTRUMENTATION, TRANSPORT EARLY rather than waiting to see, pre-alert saying inhalation injury, reassess the voice throughout.
back.why_it_matters: Everything on this card is about acting before the airway closes rather than after.

front.title: Burn management
front.summary: Rings off, nothing on, look elsewhere

back.body: REMOVE RINGS AND CONSTRICTING ITEMS EARLY — fifteen seconds now, impossible in ten minutes · LEAVE ANYTHING STUCK TO THE BURN, cut around it · DRY STERILE DRESSING AND NOTHING ELSE — no cream, ointment, butter, toothpaste or ICE · DO NOT BREAK BLISTERS — intact skin is an infection barrier · KEEP THEM WARM — they have lost the organ that holds heat in · LOOK FOR THE OTHER INJURIES — people escaping fires FALL, JUMP and get hit · SIGNIFICANT AT ANY SIZE: FACE · HANDS · FEET · GENITALIA · ACROSS A JOINT · CIRCUMFERENTIAL · Very young and very old do worse · BURN CENTRE CRITERIA ARE YOURS TO LEARN LOCALLY · Pattern not matching the story? RECORD FACTS, REPORT via safeguarding
back.why_it_matters: The burns were what you saw from the doorway. The ankle was what he needed an operation for.

back.body: FRACTURE = broken bone · DISLOCATION = joint out of position · SPRAIN = LIGAMENT stretched or torn · STRAIN = MUSCLE or TENDON · YOU CANNOT TELL A FRACTURE FROM A SPRAIN IN THE FIELD — splint it and let the x-ray decide; nobody was harmed by a splinted sprain · OPEN FRACTURE = BROKEN SKIN OVER IT, bone need NOT be visible — high infection risk, SAY THE WORD OPEN · SIGNS: deformity · swelling · bruising · point tenderness · cannot use it · crepitus — NEVER GO LOOKING FOR CREPITUS · COMPARE WITH THE OTHER SIDE · Splint angulated injuries AS FOUND unless pulseless (protocol) · A FEMUR BLEEDS INTO THE THIGH — circulation problem too · CSM BEFORE AND AFTER, every time
back.why_it_matters: It had been invisible until there was something to compare it against.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-06-05-01. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: SPLINTING: reduces PAIN · prevents further NERVE and VESSEL damage · limits BLEEDING · makes the patient MOVABLE · IMMOBILISE THE JOINT ABOVE AND THE JOINT BELOW a fractured bone (for a joint: the bone above and below) · CSM BEFORE AND IMMEDIATELY AFTER — it is the only way to tell your splint from the injury · EXPOSE and DRESS OPEN WOUNDS FIRST — you cannot dress through a splint · REMOVE RINGS distal to it · PAD THE SPLINT AND THE GAPS, especially bony points — forty minutes of pressure causes real injury · SPLINT AS FOUND unless pulseless and protocol permits · TYPES: rigid · formable · vacuum · sling and swathe · the patient's own body · MAJOR TRAUMA: MOVE FIRST, splint en route or not at all
back.why_it_matters: Five minutes of excellent care applied to the injury least likely to be the problem.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: decide splint-now versus move-now, expose and compare sides, CHECK AND RECORD CSM FIRST, dress open wounds, remove rings, immobilise joint above and below, PAD the bony points, splint AS FOUND, secure without constricting, RECHECK CSM IMMEDIATELY AFTER, recheck again in transport, document both with times.
back.why_it_matters: The two checks are the skill. Everything between them is technique.

back.body: FOR: ISOLATED · CLOSED · MID-SHAFT FEMUR — and almost nothing else · WHY IT WORKS: the thigh muscles are the strongest in the body; when the femur breaks they pull the ends PAST EACH OTHER and hold them there — that spasm is the pain, the shortening and the ongoing bleeding · TRACTION realigns and relaxes → pain drops, bleeding slows · CONTRAINDICATED: PELVIS · HIP · KNEE · ANKLE on that side · LOWER LEG FRACTURE · PARTIAL AMPUTATION · open femur per protocol · ASSESS THE PELVIS BEFORE THE SPLINT LEAVES THE LOCKER · TWO PEOPLE · MANUAL TRACTION IS NEVER RELEASED until the device holds · CSM before and after · Wrong device for a multiply injured patient
back.why_it_matters: The splint that was about to help him would have pulled open the injury that was actually bleeding.

Critical: confirm ISOLATED CLOSED MID-SHAFT femur, ASSESS THE PELVIS FIRST, rule out hip/knee/ankle/lower leg/partial amputation, CSM first, person one applies and HOLDS manual traction, person two measures and secures ischial strap and ankle hitch, apply mechanical traction, ONLY THEN release manual traction, recheck CSM, reassess in transport.
back.why_it_matters: Every contraindication is the same idea: a broken anchor means you are pulling a broken thing apart.

back.body: THE PELVIS IS A RING — it CANNOT break in only one place · find one fracture, there is a second · WHY IT BLEEDS: large vessels and a rich venous network tear, AND the displaced ring opens a space with no ceiling on it — patients EXSANGUINATE INTO THEIR OWN PELVIS · ALL OF IT IS INTERNAL, INVISIBLE AND UNREACHABLE · MECHANISMS: fall from height · motorcyclist · pedestrian · side intrusion · AND A FALL FROM STANDING IN AN OLDER PATIENT · SIGNS: pelvic/groin/back pain · instability · bruising over pelvis or perineum · leg shortened or rotated out · UNEXPLAINED SHOCK · ASSESS STABILITY ONCE, GENTLY — OR NOT AT ALL · DO NOT LOG ROLL — scoop or flat lift · BINDER EARLY, warm, minimal movement, GO
back.why_it_matters: Three people checked, all doing something reasonable, and broke up the clot three times.

back.body: CSM = CIRCULATION · SENSATION · MOVEMENT (also PMS: pulse, motor, sensory) · CIRCULATION: pulse if findable · colour · warmth · capillary refill — ALL COMPARED WITH THE OTHER SIDE · SENSATION: not 'can you feel this' but 'DOES IT FEEL THE SAME AS THE OTHER SIDE?' · MOVEMENT: wiggle the fingers or toes beyond the injury · A READING WITHOUT A COMPARISON IS NEARLY UNINTERPRETABLE · BEFORE AND AFTER EVERYTHING, WITH A TIME · WHY IT MATTERS: COMPARTMENT SYNDROME — PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION is the earliest sign · pain on passive stretch · tight woody compartment · A PRESENT PULSE EXCLUDES NOTHING, and losing it is very late · WORSE AFTER YOUR SPLINT? LOOSEN AND REASSESS NOW
back.why_it_matters: Nobody could say whether it happened in the splint, before it, or on the way in.

front.title: CSM
front.summary: The check, twice, with a clock

back.body: C — CIRCULATION: distal pulse if findable, colour, warmth, capillary refill, all compared with the other side · S — SENSATION: 'does it feel the SAME as the other side?' · M — MOVEMENT: wiggle fingers or toes beyond the injury · Also PMS: Pulse, Motor, Sensory — same three · BEFORE and AFTER every splint, bandage or move — WITH A TIME ON EACH
back.why_it_matters: The two times are what make either check mean anything.

back.body: IT CLOSES THE RING — less space for blood to fill, clot can form, ends stop grinding · APPLY ON SUSPICION — mechanism + pain, or mechanism + unexplained shock · you will never get confirmation in the field · IT GOES OVER THE GREATER TROCHANTERS — the widest bony points of the hips, roughly level with the buttock crease · NOT THE ILIAC CRESTS · NOT THE WAIST · TOO HIGH DOES NOT CLOSE THE RING AND CAN BE WORSE THAN NOTHING · EMPTY THE POCKETS FIRST — it stays on for hours · APPLY BEFORE MOVING · DO NOT LOG ROLL — slide it up from the knees, or scoop, or flat lift · TIGHTEN TO SPEC, more is not better · NEVER REMOVE OR LOOSEN IT IN THE FIELD · A folded sheet at the same LEVEL works per protocol
back.why_it_matters: The device was right, the decision was right, and the level was ten centimetres too high.

front.title: Skull fractures and scalp wounds
front.summary: The bone is the dent; the brain is the engine

back.body: SCALP BLEEDS DRAMATICALLY — rich supply, vessels HELD OPEN so they cannot retract · usually looks worse than it is, BUT significant in CHILDREN and ANTICOAGULATED patients · DIRECT PRESSURE — but only GENTLE, AROUND THE EDGES, over a suspected depressed or open fracture · NEVER PROBE A SCALP WOUND — you push fragments inward · BASILAR FRACTURE: BATTLE SIGN (behind the ear) and RACCOON EYES — BOTH TAKE HOURS, so their absence early means NOTHING · CLEAR OR BLOOD-STAINED FLUID FROM EAR OR NOSE may be CSF — look for a HALO on the dressing · DO NOT PACK — cover loosely, let it drain · THE BRAIN UNDERNEATH MATTERS MORE THAN THE BONE
back.why_it_matters: Battle sign takes hours. The halo on the dressing was there in twenty minutes.

back.body: THE SKULL IS A CLOSED BOX — swelling or blood has nowhere to go, so pressure rises · PRIMARY INJURY = the impact. DONE. Nothing changes it · SECONDARY INJURY = everything after: LOW OXYGEN · LOW BLOOD PRESSURE · rising pressure · fever · seizures — PREVENTING IT IS THE WHOLE PREHOSPITAL JOB · HYPOXIA AND HYPOTENSION WORSEN OUTCOME MOST → oxygenation and perfusion ARE the treatment · THE KEY SIGN IS A FALLING LEVEL OF CONSCIOUSNESS — repeated, with times · CUSHING TRIAD: BP UP · PULSE DOWN · BREATHING IRREGULAR — A LATE SIGN, DO NOT WAIT FOR IT · HERNIATION: fixed dilated pupil (same side) · rapid decline · posturing · Head NEUTRAL and elevated per protocol · warm · GO, and pre-alert
back.why_it_matters: Three assessments with three times said everything. Any one of them said nothing.

front.title: Head injury: the signs and their timing

back.body: CUSHING TRIAD — BP RISING · PULSE FALLING · BREATHING IRREGULAR · WHEN IT APPEARS: LATE — it confirms what consciousness already told you · THE TWO THINGS THAT WORSEN OUTCOME MOST: HYPOXIA + HYPOTENSION · THE MOST IMPORTANT SIGN: LEVEL OF CONSCIOUSNESS, REPEATED WITH TIMES — the trend, not the reading · HERNIATION PUPIL: FIXED AND DILATED, usually the injured side, with rapid decline and posturing
back.why_it_matters: Everything famous about head injury arrives late. The thing that arrives early is a patient answering worse than they did ten minutes ago.

front.title: Concussion
front.summary: You do not have to be knocked out

back.body: A BRAIN INJURY from force transmitted to the head — direct or through the body · LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS IS NOT REQUIRED and is ABSENT IN MOST — 'he never went out' is not reassurance · SIGNS: headache · confusion · dazed, slowed, foggy · dizzy · nauseated · blurred or double vision · light and noise sensitivity · out of character emotionally · AMNESIA AROUND THE EVENT — ask what they last remember before and first after · REPEATING THE SAME QUESTION is often what bystanders notice first · SYMPTOMS EVOLVE OVER HOURS — looking well is NOT being cleared · STOP THE ACTIVITY, NO RETURN THAT DAY · A SECOND IMPACT BEFORE RECOVERY CAN BE CATASTROPHIC · RED FLAGS: worsening headache · repeated vomiting · seizure · increasing drowsiness · weakness · slurred speech · falling consciousness
back.why_it_matters: He had asked his teammate the score twice in ninety seconds, and the coach had watched it happen.

front.title: Eye, ear and dental injuries
front.summary: Both eyes, inner to outer, by the crown

back.body: THE EYES MOVE TOGETHER → COVER BOTH for any serious injury to one · EXPLAIN FIRST AND KEEP TALKING — sudden blindness is frightening · IMPALED OBJECT IN AN EYE: NEVER REMOVE, stabilise without pressure, cover both · CHEMICAL: IRRIGATE IMMEDIATELY AND AT LENGTH — FROM THE INNER CORNER OUTWARDS, AWAY FROM THE OTHER EYE · get the direction wrong and one injured eye becomes two · DISPLACED EYEBALL: do NOT replace — moist sterile dressing + shield · AVULSED TOOTH: HOLD BY THE CROWN, NEVER THE ROOT · do not scrub · KEEP IT MOIST (milk or saliva per protocol) · bring it · check it is not in the airway · EARS: DO NOT PACK THE CANAL
back.why_it_matters: The instinct to irrigate fast was right. The direction turned one injured eye into two.

front.title: Neck injuries
front.summary: Never wrap anything around a neck

back.body: EVERYTHING RUNS THROUGH THE NECK in a small space with no protection · OPEN WOUND INTO A LARGE VEIN CAN DRAW AIR IN — rapidly fatal · OCCLUSIVE DRESSING: keeps air OUT and holds pressure · DIRECT PRESSURE ON THE WOUND · NEVER CIRCUMFERENTIAL — you would compress the AIRWAY and the OTHER CAROTID · USE YOUR HAND; if it must be secured, OVER THE DRESSING AND UNDER THE OPPOSITE ARMPIT · EXPANDING SWELLING CLOSES AIRWAYS OVER MINUTES — watch it continuously, LISTEN TO THE VOICE · AIRWAY INJURY: hoarseness · trouble swallowing · AIR BUBBLING from the wound · CRACKLING under the skin · Assume spinal injury, but airway and bleeding come first · GO EARLY
back.why_it_matters: The bandage was holding the dressing beautifully, and compressing the airway and the other carotid.

front.title: Spinal motion restriction
front.summary: The patient decides, not the mechanism

back.body: SELECTIVE, NOT UNIVERSAL · WHY IT CHANGED: boards cause PRESSURE INJURY within under an hour · pain → MORE movement · restricted breathing · difficult airway, especially if they vomit — with THIN evidence of benefit · CRITERIA CONSIDER: altered mental status · intoxication · NEUROLOGICAL DEFICIT · MIDLINE tenderness (over the spine, NOT the muscle beside it) · DISTRACTING INJURY · Alert, sober, no deficit, no midline tenderness, no distracting injury = generally NOT indicated, however dramatic the crash · USE YOUR OWN PROTOCOL'S CRITERIA · GOAL IS MINIMISING MOVEMENT, NOT RIGIDITY · THE BOARD IS AN EXTRICATION DEVICE · MANUAL IN-LINE STABILISATION IS THE FOUNDATION
back.why_it_matters: Two hands on a head costs nothing, harms nobody, and is the best spinal precaution you have.

back.body: See the algorithm card. Manual in-line stabilisation first and throughout. Then: altered or intoxicated? neurological deficit? MIDLINE tenderness? distracting injury? A yes at any point means restrict per protocol. All four no means restriction is generally not indicated — and document each criterion you assessed.
back.why_it_matters: The mechanism is not one of the boxes. That is the whole change.

back.body: A CORD INJURY CUTS THE NERVES THAT KEEP VESSELS CONSTRICTED → everything below dilates · NO BLOOD IS LOST — THE CONTAINER GREW · distribution problem, not volume · SKIN: WARM · DRY · FLUSHED — because the nerves that would clamp it are cut · PULSE: NORMAL OR SLOW — because the nerves that would speed it are cut · CLASSIC: hypotensive trauma patient, SLOW pulse, WARM DRY skin — everything backwards from normal shock · NEVER ASSUME IT UNTIL BLEEDING IS EXCLUDED — whatever broke the spine can break a spleen · THEY LOSE TEMPERATURE CONTROL — cold fast, blanket them early · SPINAL SHOCK IS DIFFERENT: loss of CORD FUNCTION below the injury, not a circulation problem
back.why_it_matters: He fell far enough to break his spine, which is far enough to break a spleen.

front.title: Hemorrhagic vs neurogenic shock
front.summary: Cool and fast, or warm and slow

back.body: See the comparison rows. Hemorrhagic: volume lost, PALE COOL CLAMMY, FAST weak pulse. Neurogenic: container enlarged, WARM DRY FLUSHED, NORMAL OR SLOW pulse, temperature control lost. Assume the first; conclude the second only after excluding it.
back.why_it_matters: Everything about neurogenic shock is the opposite of what shock is supposed to look like.

front.title: Helmet removal
front.summary: Take the head before the helmet leaves

back.body: HELMETS USUALLY STAY ON · LEAVE IT IF: airway clear and manageable · fits SNUGLY · head can be immobilised in it · REMOVE IT IF: it blocks the AIRWAY · it is LOOSE (head moves inside, so it stabilises nothing) · it PREVENTS IMMOBILISATION · CARDIAC ARREST · ALWAYS TWO PEOPLE · Visor and glasses off, chin strap undone, SPREAD THE SIDES to clear ears and nose · THE WHOLE SKILL IS THE HANDOVER: person one CHANGES HOLD AND TAKES THE HEAD FROM BELOW before the helmet clears · PAD BEHIND THE HEAD afterwards — without the helmet it sits low · SPORTS HELMET? See if the FACEMASK alone comes off · SHOULDER PADS: BOTH OR NEITHER · SLOWLY, and stop for resistance or change
back.why_it_matters: The helmet had been doing that job the entire time, and it stopped the instant it came off.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: decide whether it needs to come off at all, check whether a FACEMASK alone will do, get a SECOND PERSON, person one stabilises from the sides, unfasten the strap, SPREAD the sides, PERSON ONE CHANGES HOLD TO TAKE THE HEAD FROM BELOW, ease it off, PAD BEHIND THE HEAD, helmet and shoulder pads BOTH OR NEITHER, stop for resistance or neurological change, reassess and document.
back.why_it_matters: There is no version of this that should be done quickly.

back.body: THE PAIN IS THE PROBLEM — it stops deep breathing → collapse → secretions → PNEUMONIA · real mortality, especially in older patients · NEVER STRAP OR BIND A CHEST — it relieves pain by preventing the exact breathing that keeps them alive · ENCOURAGE DEEP BREATHS AND COUGHING, supported with their own arm or a pillow · UPPER ribs = substantial force · LOWER ribs = think LIVER (right) and SPLEEN (left) · FLAIL CHEST = 3+ RIBS BROKEN IN 2+ PLACES EACH → a segment disconnected from the rib cage · IT FOLLOWS THE PRESSURE INSIDE, not the chest: IN on inspiration, OUT on expiration · MUSCLE SPASM CAN HIDE IT FOR AN HOUR · THE PULMONARY CONTUSION UNDERNEATH IS WHAT HARMS THEM — oxygen, watch the breathing, support it, GO
back.why_it_matters: The ribs had been broken the whole time. The muscles were splinting it until they got tired.

back.body: PNEUMOTHORAX = air between lung and chest wall → the lung falls away and collapses · SIGNS: short of breath · pain worse on breathing in · REDUCED OR ABSENT BREATH SOUNDS ON ONE SIDE (compare both) · TENSION: a ONE-WAY FLAP lets air IN each breath and not OUT → pressure builds → lung collapses fully → THE MIDDLE OF THE CHEST IS PUSHED ACROSS → THE GREAT VEINS KINK → BLOOD STOPS RETURNING = OBSTRUCTIVE SHOCK · IT PRESENTS AS BREATHING AND KILLS AS CIRCULATION · NECK VEINS AND TRACHEAL DEVIATION ARE LATE AND OFTEN ABSENT — DO NOT WAIT · BAGGING A SIMPLE PNEUMOTHORAX CAN CREATE A TENSION · YOUR ACTION: RELEASE ANY OCCLUSIVE DRESSING · high-flow O2 · GO · pre-alert
back.why_it_matters: Every squeeze was pushing air into a space that could not empty.

front.title: Simple vs tension pneumothorax
front.summary: The blood pressure is the tell

back.body: See the comparison rows. The finding that separates them is the BLOOD PRESSURE: a simple pneumothorax does not drop it, a tension does. Do not wait for neck veins or a deviated trachea — both are late and often never appear.
back.why_it_matters: Severe distress plus absent breath sounds on one side plus a falling pressure is the whole diagnosis.

front.title: Open chest wounds
front.summary: A door that only opens outwards

back.body: AIR ENTERS THROUGH THE WOUND INSTEAD OF THE AIRWAY → the lung collapses · 'Sucking chest wound' is the SOUND · bubbling or frothy blood · TREAT WITH A VENTED CHEST SEAL — the ONE-WAY VALVE keeps air OUT while letting trapped air OUT · A PLAIN FOUR-SIDED DRESSING SEALS BOTH WAYS AND CAN CREATE A TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX · Only plain available? TAPE ON THREE SIDES per protocol — the free edge is a homemade valve · CHECK THE BACK, SIDES AND ARMPITS BEFORE SEALING — exit wounds need sealing too · NEVER PACK A CHEST WOUND · AFTER SEALING, WATCH FOR TENSION — rising distress, falling pressure → LIFT A CORNER, VENT, REAPPLY · Sit them up, high-flow O2, GO
back.why_it_matters: Sitting him forward for five seconds would have found the second wound.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: recognise it, CHECK THE BACK AND SIDES FIRST, seal with a VENTED seal (or three-sided tape per protocol), seal EVERY wound you found, do NOT pack, high-flow oxygen, sit them up, WATCH FOR TENSION after sealing, and if it develops LIFT A CORNER, VENT AND REAPPLY immediately.
back.why_it_matters: You can cause a tension pneumothorax with a dressing, and you can reverse it by lifting a corner.

back.body: HEMOTHORAX = BLOOD in the space around the lung → lung COLLAPSES *and* blood LEAVES THE CIRCULATION · BREATHING SIGNS *PLUS* SHOCK — that combination is how you tell it from a pneumothorax · The chest holds a LOT — litres lost with nothing visible · TAMPONADE = blood in the SAC around the heart, which CANNOT STRETCH → the heart CONTRACTS FINE BUT CANNOT FILL → each beat ejects less · BECK TRIAD (muffled sounds, distended neck veins, low pressure) IS LATE AND USUALLY INCOMPLETE — you will not hear muffled sounds in a moving ambulance · SUSPECT IT FROM: SHOCK + CENTRAL PENETRATING WOUND + CLEAR LUNG SOUNDS · WOUND SIZE MEANS NOTHING · NEITHER IS TREATABLE BY YOU: oxygen, warm, position, GO, PRE-ALERT
back.why_it_matters: The clear lungs were the finding. They argued against the chest, which left the heart.

back.body: See the comparison rows. The separating finding is the breath sounds: REDUCED on one side points at blood in the chest; CLEAR on BOTH sides in a shocked patient with a central wound points at the heart. Both get the same treatment from you: oxygen, warmth, position, and speed.
back.why_it_matters: A fingertip-sized wound in the middle of the chest is a classic tamponade.

back.body: SOLID ORGANS (liver, spleen, kidneys) BLEED — the usual cause of shock · HOLLOW ORGANS (bowel, stomach, bladder) LEAK → peritonitis over HOURS · BOTH ARE INVISIBLE FROM OUTSIDE · BLUNT ABDOMINAL TRAUMA CAN BE COMPLETELY OCCULT — a SOFT ABDOMEN EARLY IS NOT REASSURANCE, rigidity takes time · READ THE MECHANISM AND THE VITALS: handlebars · SEATBELT MARK · fall from height · lower rib fractures · + rising pulse, falling pressure · ANY WOUND BETWEEN THE NIPPLES AND THE GROIN may have entered — including FLANK and BACK · EVISCERATION: NEVER PUSH THEM BACK IN · MOIST STERILE DRESSING then an OCCLUSIVE LAYER — dried bowel dies · no pressure on the organs · KNEES BENT · nothing by mouth · warm · GO
back.why_it_matters: If the belt marked the skin, the force went into whatever was behind it.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: NEVER push the organs back in, no pressure on them, control bleeding at the wound edges only, MOIST sterile dressing first, OCCLUSIVE layer over it, nothing that sticks or sheds fibres, supine with KNEES BENT, nothing by mouth, keep warm, check for other wounds including the back, expedite and pre-alert.
back.why_it_matters: Exposed bowel dries quickly, and dried bowel dies. The moist layer keeps it alive.

back.body: A BLOW TO THE CHEST AT EXACTLY THE WRONG MOMENT stops a COMPLETELY NORMAL HEART · No heart disease · usually NO CHEST INJURY AT ALL, often not even a mark · THE BLOW NEED NOT BE HARD — a ball, a puck, an elbow · TIMING is what matters: a window of MILLISECONDS in the electrical cycle → VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION · Same blow a fraction earlier or later does nothing, which is why it is rare · MOSTLY CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS — more flexible chests transmit the force · ANYONE WHO COLLAPSES AFTER A BLOW TO THE CHEST IS IN ARREST UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE — NOT WINDED · IMMEDIATE CPR + DEFIBRILLATION AS EARLY AS POSSIBLE · do NOT examine the chest first · These hearts work perfectly again if restarted
back.why_it_matters: They gave him a minute to get his breath back. It lasted ninety seconds and cost him something.

front.title: Prioritising injuries
front.summary: The loudest injury rarely matters most

back.body: MULTI-SYSTEM = injuries COMPETING for your attention · THE MOST VISIBLE INJURY IS OFTEN NOT THE MOST DANGEROUS — a bent forearm, a bleeding scalp and a burn all shout; a RIGID ABDOMEN, a TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX and a DETERIORATING HEAD INJURY do not · PRIORITIES FOLLOW THE PRIMARY ASSESSMENT: catastrophic bleeding → AIRWAY → BREATHING → CIRCULATION → DISABILITY → EXPOSURE · MINUTES OUTRANK HOURS · WORK IN PARALLEL, NOT IN SEQUENCE — say out loud who is doing what · long scene times come from taking turns, not from being slow · REASSESS — the priority changes as the patient does · DECIDE THE DESTINATION EARLY, it shapes everything · WHAT YOU DO NOT DO IS ALSO A DECISION
back.why_it_matters: The arm was the loudest injury in the room and the one that mattered least.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-06-08-01. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: GETTING THEM OUT FAST with MANUAL stabilisation only, accepting MORE spinal movement · IT IS A TRADE: a POSSIBLE spinal injury against a DEFINITE immediate threat · THREE INDICATIONS: (1) UNSAFE SCENE — fire, unstable vehicle, live traffic, hostility, rising water · (2) UNSTABLE PATIENT — airway you cannot manage there, uncontrolled bleeding, falling consciousness — because the injury they HAVE will kill them before the one they MIGHT have · (3) ACCESS TO ANOTHER CRITICAL PATIENT · NOT INDICATIONS: being ready · being in a hurry · the weather · MANUAL IN-LINE STABILISATION CONTINUES THROUGHOUT — imperfect but continuous · THE BOARD IS FOR MOVING, NOT TRANSPORTING · SAY IT OUT LOUD AND DOCUMENT WHY
back.why_it_matters: There are three indications. Being ready is not one, and it is the commonest reason it gets done.

front.title: Rapid extrication decision
front.summary: Three boxes, and none of them is 'hurry'

back.body: See the algorithm card. Unsafe scene? Unstable patient? Access to another critical patient? A yes to any means rapid extrication with continuous manual stabilisation, said out loud and documented. All three no means a careful staged extrication.
back.why_it_matters: A rapid extrication with a documented reason is a clinical decision. One without is something that just happened.

back.body: PRIMARY = THE PRESSURE WAVE → AIR-FILLED ORGANS: LUNGS · EARS · BOWEL · BLAST LUNG can show ALMOST NOTHING at first and DEVELOP OVER HOURS · SECONDARY = DEBRIS AND FRAGMENTS → penetrating trauma — THE COMMONEST CAUSE OF CASUALTIES · TERTIARY = THE BODY THROWN → blunt, fractures, crush · QUATERNARY = EVERYTHING ELSE: burns · inhalation · toxic · worsening of existing conditions · ONE PATIENT COMMONLY HAS SEVERAL · INTACT EARDRUMS EXCLUDE NOTHING — blast lung occurs with them intact · REASSESS OVER TIME · SCENE: SECONDARY DEVICES TARGET RESPONDERS · collapse · fire · DO NOT ENTER until declared safe, and watch where you assemble
back.why_it_matters: He walked out without a mark on him. It took two hours for the lungs to show it.

front.title: Trauma in pregnancy
front.summary: Treat her, and you have treated both

back.body: THE BEST TREATMENT FOR THE BABY IS RESUSCITATING THE MOTHER — there is no separate fetal treatment available to you · INCREASED BLOOD VOLUME → she loses a LOT before her vitals change · BLOOD IS DIVERTED AWAY FROM THE UTERUS BEFORE SHE SHOWS ANY SIGN → A NORMAL MATERNAL BP IS NOT REASSURANCE ABOUT THE PREGNANCY · AFTER ABOUT MID-PREGNANCY, LYING FLAT LETS THE UTERUS COMPRESS THE VEIN RETURNING BLOOD TO THE HEART → the pressure drops from POSITION ALONE · TILT HER LEFT, or manually displace the uterus left · SPINAL PRECAUTIONS? TILT THE WHOLE DEVICE · PLACENTAL SEPARATION can follow MODEST trauma and may have NO pain, NO contractions and NO bleeding · ASSESS EVERY PREGNANT TRAUMA PATIENT, however well she seems
back.why_it_matters: Her pressure came back before they reached the end of the road.
